Light and Fatigue in the Short Drama Factory The yellow earth of the Bailu Plain in Xi’an had been beaten into sticky mud by relentless, cold rain. Thirty-odd crew members huddled under a draughty, faux-antique colonnade, squatting on their heels while shoveling down souring thirteen-yuan boxed meals of stewed cabbage and fat pork. Before the downpour had fully slackened, director Wang Jing ground her cheap cigarette stub into the mud and rasped an order across the courtyard: the call sheet demanded twenty-two scenes wrapped before dawn; miss one, and not a single soul on set would close their eyes tonight.
Polyester Robes in the Mud and Bloodshot Eyes # Late-autumn winds across the Loess Plateau cut straight down open collars. Beneath the dripping eaves of the faux-Ming courtyard, temporary yellow power cables lay coiled like disemboweled intestines in the mire. Two pairs of two-kilowatt tungsten lamps, rigged beside a tarp lean-to, washed the sheets of rain in a sterile, chalky glare.
The twenty-two-year-old male lead wore a synthetic dragon robe bought wholesale from Taobao. The scarlet polyester was paper-thin; its hem had soaked up gallons of yellow silt water, clinging heavy and sodden against his thermal long johns, reeking of industrial chemical dyes mixed with rainwater. His eyes were mapped with a spiderweb of raw, blood-red veins, both eyelids swollen like overripe purple plums—the biological toll of working twenty-two hours without sleep. A makeup assistant clutched a fraying, shed-hair brush, grinding cakey foundation onto the peeling skin around his lips. Sweat and rainwater curdled the makeup into chalky ravines along his nasolabial folds.
“All departments ready! Scene two, take one!”
Director Wang Jing sat on an overturned plastic milk crate wrapped in a grimy black down parka, throat raspy with dry coughs. The monitor beside her had been replaced with a dedicated vertical display showing three squashed camera feeds. There was no blocking, no rehearsal, not even an explanation of the plot. Wang Jing gestured frantically into the rain: “Patriarch strikes from across the void! Move faster! Raise the right arm, put steel in your eyes, grit your teeth and scream! Post will drop in the lightning bolts later. When that slap lands, the supporting actress drops immediately—do not drag it out, make the fall sharp!”
The actress opposite him balanced a collapsing plastic hair bun, its adhesive dissolving in the rain, stinging her eyes until tears cut clean tracks through her rouge. The clapperboard snapped. Her face instantly twisted into a vicious sneer; right on cue, she absorbed the invisible blow, hurling herself flat into the yellow slush. Freezing wastewater soaked straight through her thin silk qipao.
Two minutes later, the safety take was in the can. Before the actor could wipe the grime from his cheekbones, a production runner yanked him into a drafty canvas tent. Within three minutes, he was stripped of the wet robe, shoved into a pill-covered polyester suit, handed a clip-on silk tie, and propelled into an adjacent partitioned room dubbed the “Billionaire Patriarch’s Corner Office” to bellow out another round of vengeance and humiliation.
This city pumps out thousands of such productions every month. One hundred episodes shot in seven days, cut in twenty-four hours, pushed onto live ad feeds the following morning. Across the loess bluffs of Xi’an and the barren river flats of Zhengzhou, tens of thousands of young bodies churn under tarps and mud, rotating like cattle on an industrial slaughter line.
Algorithmic Leeches and the Ninety-Percent Ledger # Industry press releases and venture-capital decks brim with vulgar tales of instant fortune: “Ten million yuan in billings within twenty-four hours,” “Helicopter production costs recouped in eight days,” “Financial freedom off a single two-hundred-thousand-yuan wager.”
None of these myths survive a five-minute inspection of an actual general ledger. When a breakout hit touts single-day top-ups surpassing ten million yuan, the platform dashboard flashes green, but the production boss feels cold sweat on his palms.
In the fraction of a second when a scrolling user is hooked by a manufactured cliffhanger and taps the paywall prompt, between eighty-five and ninety-two percent of that payment is immediately routed via programmatic interfaces directly into the ad-bidding accounts of ByteDance and Tencent. The platforms are algorithmic leeches clamped tight against the windpipe of the business. Media-buying teams in southern high-rises stare at trading terminals like pit bosses at a baccarat table: pump one yuan into user acquisition, and if top-ups yield one yuan and three cents, the ROI curve is positive; automated bidding scripts scale the leverage instantly, burning through tens of thousands of dollars an hour. The moment conversion rates stumble—returning ninety-eight cents on the dollar—the media buyer pulls the plug within thirty seconds, leaving the production to rot silently in the dead zones of the recommendation feed.
What trickles down to the shooting crews in Xi’an and Zhengzhou is a mere five to eight percent production service fee.
An eighty-thousand-yuan total budget must cover soundstages, lighting rentals, forty boxed meals a day, wardrobe wear-and-tear, and the wages of every soul on set. Leads take home several hundred to a thousand yuan a day in hard cash; gaffers wear through two pairs of canvas shoes lugging iron stands across mud; rough-cut editors splicing together eighty episodes of screaming and slapping walk away with royalties that barely cover a packet of cheap cigarettes. As detailed in our examination of the realities of bottom-tier labor and expendable human collateral, the moment physiological stamina is treated as bulk industrial feedstock, the irreversible depreciation of the human frame is accounted for as a zero-cost marginal consumable.
It is a blood sport: tens of thousands of cases of chronic gastritis, corneal ulcers, and spinal degeneration fed into the furnace to keep the cash flow of tech monopolies humming.
Vertical Assembly Lines in Shell Buildings # Five hundred kilometers to the east, Zhengzhou has refined this vertical assembly line into an even more ruthlessly mechanized template.
In abandoned industrial parks across the southern and western suburbs, tens of thousands of square meters of unfinished shell towers and shuttered hardware mills have been carved up with cheap drywall. An entire floor is partitioned into a micro-universe of cardboard grandeur: to the left, an engagement ballroom draped in stained red satin; to the right, an intensive care ward patched together with two secondhand hospital beds and decommissioned heart monitors; around the corridor, an executive suite assembled from veneer laminate desks.
Along the narrow, unlit hallway running between them, twenty crews shoot simultaneously throughout the night. The stagnant air is thick with stale cigarette tar, damp gypsum dust, synthetic hairspray fumes, and the sour reek of leftover instant noodle broth decomposing in garbage bins.
From the east end comes a frantic shout: “Three years of exile have ended—kneel to greet the Dragon King!” From the west end rings the shatter of dropped porcelain: “Sign these divorce papers and get out of our family!” Gaffers trade curses over jury-rigged breaker boxes to keep their lights from tripping the mains.
There is no room here for dramatic pacing, let alone aesthetic stillness. The assembly line operates according to strict anatomical metrics:
Every drama is dissected into eighty to one hundred episodes, each timed between eighty and one hundred seconds. The first three seconds must present torn clothing, a pointed pistol, or an open-handed slap to pin down the thumb; By the thirtieth second, the protagonist must suffer total humiliation, with boots planted firmly on their neck; At the sixtieth second, the counterattack begins to surface; At the ninetieth second, the episode snaps shut at peak tension, dead-center on a prompt demanding sixty cents to unlock the next ninety seconds. This is targeted electroconvulsive therapy for the human neurotransmitter system. It does not produce stories; it mines dopamine at maximum velocity.
In crowded editing suites across Zhengzhou, hundreds of twenty-somethings sit packed in front of blue monitors. The clatter of their keyboards matches the cadence of industrial sewing machines. Junior editors must chew through two thousand minutes of raw footage a day; cinematic theory learned in vocational school is useless dead weight. They need remember only three mechanical laws: heavy beats demand metal impact sound effects, narrative turns require crash zooms, and emotional peaks require wall-to-wall sub-bass rumbles.
When inland manufacturing fails to provide viable work, as chronicled in our report on the contraction of county economies and youth migration, this vertical workshop born of ad-traffic arbitrage becomes the sole refuge for vocational graduates and cast-off extras from the dying studios of Hengdian.
The Wrap Order in the Mud # The collapse of the bubble came not as a slow leak, but with the sudden finality of a guillotine blade.
Regulatory orders dropped at midnight, purging vulgar mini-program portals overnight. Major tech platforms seized the opening to force a free, ad-supported revenue-share model, using proprietary distribution algorithms to swallow the outsized margins once claimed by pay-per-episode producers. Top-up revenue pools collapsed from tens of millions to mere hundreds of thousands; the net split left to independent studios became paper-thin.
Around the night-market skewers in southern Xi’an, the bombastic “Hit Alliance” fell silent. No one boasted of penalty toasts for failing to break ten million on day one. Conversations sank into hushed reckonings: which outfit sank six hundred thousand yuan into an original series only to claw back six hundred yuan in net splits, whose gear had been seized by predatory microlenders, and which editor had passed out coughing blood at their desk after seventy straight hours of crunch.
At four-thirty in the morning, the wind howling across the bluffs of the Bailu Plain sounded like a cracked bellows. The temperature had plunged near freezing.
The rain continued without pause, filling muddy hollows with black diesel scum. Behind a dripping tarp, a generator sputtered, belching plumes of choking bluish exhaust.
The twenty-two-year-old actor, wrapped in a threadbare army coat emptied of down feathers, squatted by a mud hole, coughing violently as his narrow shoulders shook in the biting draft. He had just spent forty straight minutes kneeling in ice water; his joints were stiff and unresponsive. Ten yards away, an assistant director lifted an electric megaphone, his voice hoarse: “Positions! One more for safety, and we wrap!”
The actor did not hesitate. He flicked his cigarette butt into the puddle, wiped a muddy hand across his face, stumbled upright, and dropped back down into the freezing slush.
Inside this rattling factory, no one harbors any remaining illusions about the trade, but neither does anyone possess the capital to step away. Rain flecks the camera lens; someone wipes it with a dirty rag, and the shutter rolls. Dawn is approaching, and the call sheet for the next eighty-episode order has already landed in the group chat. The world has foreclosed every exit, leaving behind only this vertical machine that never sleeps.
summary: Light and Fatigue in the Short Drama Factory The yellow earth of the Bailu Plain in Xi’an had been beaten into sticky mud by relentless, cold rain. Thirty-odd crew members huddled under a draughty, faux-antique colonnade, squatting on their heels while shoveling down souring thirteen-yuan boxed meals of stewed cabbage and fat pork. Before the downpour had fully slackened, director Wang Jing ground her cheap cigarette stub into the mud and rasped an order across the courtyard: the call sheet demanded twenty-two scenes wrapped before dawn; miss one, and not a single soul on set would close their eyes tonight.
title: Light and Fatigue in the Short Drama Factory

content:
Across more than two thousand Chinese county towns, an irreversible systemic hemorrhaging is underway. This is no cyclical economic dip, but a physical contraction engineered by the dual forces of demographic siphon pumps and the receding tide of land finance.
The speed of the unraveling outpaces expectation. Once heralded by grand developmental narratives as the “sponge of urbanization,” the county seat has neither caught the retreating urban youth nor stabilized the foundations of rural society. With the tides of speculative momentum fully ebbed, all that remains is a hollow, decaying shell.
Decaying Avenues: Rusted Shutters and Stationary Traffic Lights # At noon, the traffic signals at the central crossroads mechanically switch between red, amber, and green, yet not a single vehicle traverses the desolate asphalt.
Along the main avenue, two-story commercial storefronts once proudly sported bright red banners shouting “Prime Shop for Transfer.” Today, those signs have washed away into faded shreds, exposing corroded metal rolling shutters peeling with rust. Jammed into the crevices are yellowed utility cut-off warnings, locksmith stickers, and court-stamped asset seizure notices.
The underground shopping concourses built a decade ago under the banner of “shantytown redevelopment” have seen their central air conditioners frozen for three years due to unpaid electric bills. Cardboard boxes rot in piles near the entrance, and the corridors have reverted to their original damp nature as civil air-raid shelters. Two or three white-haired elders sit in the drafty shadows of the stairwell, silently fingering weathered playing cards under faint emergency lighting.
Along the curbs rest rows of crookedly parked, off-brand electric scooters. Their synthetic leather seats are torn open by feral cats, and their brittle plastic canopies are layered with inches of coal dust and grit. Rusted ignition barrels suggest their owners packed vinyl bags two years ago and took slow trains south to screw brackets on Yangtze River assembly lines or deliver takeout along metropolitan beltways, never to turn these keys again.
The only sign of commercial life is a clearance outlet blaring discount slogans from a tinny loudspeaker on repeat. Except for idle drifters pausing to listen, the entire district resembles a black-and-white specimen played at half-speed.
Shuttered Classrooms: Villages Without Bells # Far more harrowing than empty storefronts is the complete collapse of the local education ecology.
A few years ago, every township of reasonable scale maintained a central elementary school built of red brick and reinforced concrete. Today, heavy chains and rusted padlocks wrap the iron gates. Weeds have burst through the cracked concrete playground, standing waist-high. Weather-beaten concrete ping-pong tables serve as drying platforms for corn cobs and abandoned tractor parts, while the pulley at the top of the flagpole has seized solid.
The entire county’s annual newborn headcount can no longer fill two classes at the county’s flagship experimental primary school.
Young parents, draining three generations of life savings and taking on thirty-year mortgages, have dragged their children into county test schools or municipal prep academies. Township teaching posts were erased within years under the sterile bureaucratic label of “consolidation.”
Without children running with satchels, the breakfast stalls and stationery shops in rural market towns vanished within twelve months. In villages where the school bells have fallen silent, only toothless elders sit beneath eaves, watching the final afternoon bus rumble away into the dust at three o’clock.
The biological transmission line of life has been severed at the root.
The Parasitic Loop: Eight Hundred Insiders and a Threadbare Economy # Stripped of real-estate mania and phantom investment drives, the county economy reveals its brutal essence: it possesses zero self-generating economic blood.
There is no high-value manufacturing, no shipping containers bound for overseas ports, and no fertile ground for technology start-ups. The solitary cash generator for the entire jurisdiction is the treasury payroll account at the county finance bureau on the tenth of every month.
A few hundred civil servants, public school teachers, and county hospital medical staff constitute the only class on this soil with reliable purchasing power.
The county’s internal commerce has devolved into a hyper-narrow, incestuous loop:
Bureau chiefs sign dining tabs at the two remaining business banqueting halls; Bureaucratic families swipe subsidized medical insurance cards at pharmacy chains and supermarkets run by mayoral relatives; Children attend illicit tutoring sessions run by elite public school instructors. This is a parasitic system kept alive exclusively by fiscal transfer payments. Young people who returned from first-tier cities expecting to mount a “hometown revival” with third-wave espresso cafes or artisanal bakeries were crushed within months. County seats require neither aesthetic refinement nor operational efficiency; they demand named uncles sitting in administrative compound offices and ironclad political protection over monopolies in gravel, passenger transport, and funeral services.
As observed in the shifting realities of employment and structural contraction, when labor ceases to be hunger-bought by industrial machinery, lying flat is not youthful rebellion, but the only remaining terminus.
Those capable of testing out into provincial capitals fled long ago. Those left behind are casual laborers clinging to the edges of the state apparatus, and an aging population killing time in mahjong parlors.
The Mirage of Debt and the Severed Bloodline # For over a decade, county administrations maintained an illusion of prosperity through magical local government financing vehicles (LGFVs).
Impoverished counties collecting two to three hundred million yuan in annual tax revenue racked up tens of billions in off-balance-sheet debt, bulldozing eight-lane ceremonial avenues, palatial civic administrative complexes, and weed-choked “high-tech industrial zones.” Those glass towers and neoclassical arches were never meant for production; their only utility was to supply inspectable evidence of political achievement for ascending party bosses.
The performance art has broken down.
Residential plots pass through repeated rounds of auctions without a single private bid, and LGFVs cannot roll over the interest on their bonds. Crucially, the fiscal transfers that once flowed uninterrupted are encountering rigorous audit crackdowns.
As analyzed in the central-local tug-of-war behind the new petition rules, the political center has resolved to cut off debt-bailout fantasies, forcing non-performing obligations and social liabilities back down onto local authorities.
Cut off from capital infusions and policy transfusions, the county resembles a terminal patient whose IV lines have been pulled. Municipal infrastructure financed by debt is morphing into an unsupportable maintenance nightmare. Streetlights are lit only every third post, sanitation wages shrink, and county transit fleets halt operations due to fuel insolvency.
Once the stem cells run dry, systemic tissue necrosis is merely a matter of time.
Refusing Sentimentalism: Staring into the Physical Retraction # Literary romantics are fond of draping the decay of the county seat in nostalgic pastoral gauze, spinning illusions that urban casualties can find spiritual refuge among rustic orchards.
This is hollow, bourgeois self-indulgence.
What is occurring on the ground is a cold physical shrinkage and abandonment. This is not a return to nature, but the collapse of civilizational infrastructure once maintenance becomes unaffordable: municipal pipes burst without the funds to dig them up, winter central heating gets cut off early due to municipal coal debts, and bus lines are permanently deregistered for lack of riders.
Over the coming two decades, the majority of Chinese counties lacking resource monopolies or geographic moats will undergo irreversible administrative demotion and consolidation. They will wither from counties into towns, from towns into desolated settlements, and ultimately be reclaimed by scrub pine and windblown dust.
Modern civilization is an expensive luxury contingent on extreme resource concentration. When powerful demographic siphon pumps pull the last cohort of able-bodied youth into coastal megacities, and when fiscal pipelines are cut, the final curtain on the county economy is a physical inevitability requiring no eulogy.
No emotion is called for; no sentimentality is owed. Under the unyielding laws of gravity, a retreat is simply a retreat.
summary:
Across more than two thousand Chinese county towns, an irreversible systemic hemorrhaging is underway. This is no cyclical economic dip, but a physical contraction engineered by the dual forces of demographic siphon pumps and the receding tide of land finance.
The speed of the unraveling outpaces expectation. Once heralded by grand developmental narratives as the “sponge of urbanization,” the county seat has neither caught the retreating urban youth nor stabilized the foundations of rural society. With the tides of speculative momentum fully ebbed, all that remains is a hollow, decaying shell.
title: Twilight of the County Towns: The Silent Curtain on Demographic Drain and Fiscal Retreat

content:
The presentation slides at tech keynotes are always immaculate. Bathed in cool hues of cyan and clean white, tailored executives gesture smoothly beneath the spotlights, unveiling high-frame-rate b-roll of six-axis robotic arms dancing across cleanrooms and unmanned shearers cleaving coal seams in the bowels of the earth. The official press releases are draped in immaculate corporate dignity: “Zero-Harm Production,” “Automated Hazard Mitigation,” “Upgrading the Workforce Through Intelligent Infrastructure.”
Applause ripples through the auditorium. Commentators celebrate a triumph of humanitarian progress: human beings will no longer be crushed under collapsing rock faces, nor will they gamble their marrow against the freezing crosswinds of high-rise scaffolding just to secure their next meal.
Yet no one ever asks where those who used to wager their lives for bread are supposed to go, once the spotlights pivot away and leave them in the dark.
The Final Collateral: Pricing Human Suffering and Flesh # Throughout the long, grim, grease-stained chronicle of human industrialization, manual laborers at the margins always carried a final bargaining chip no creditor could confiscate: the biological threshold of their own endurance.
It was a sordid, brutal transaction, but it was, at the very least, a recognized market.
Descending eight hundred meters into a coal seam meant turning your pulmonary alveoli into a dust filter for the mine, propping up fractured roof timber with your spine, and coughing up a mouthful of stubborn, coal-black phlegm upon surfacing at four-thirty in the morning. Tying rebar under forty-degree heat meant tightrope-walking iron beams dozens of meters in the air against gut-wrenching crosswinds, where rusted iron wire punctured through canvas gloves, festering with sweat into blackened calluses across your palms. Pouring raw chemical catalysts into explosion-proof reactors meant trading hepatic and renal longevity against the acrid stench of dimethylbenzene. Even on the night shift assembly line, one mortgaged the focal elasticity of one’s retinas and the tendon sheaths of one’s wrists in exchange for piece-rate compensation wired to a bank card at eight o’clock sharp the following morning.
In polite society, this was sanitized as “a willingness to endure hardship.”
Capital tolerated this primal barter not out of benevolence, but out of cold thermodynamic calculus: in an era when servo motors were clunky, sensors prohibitively expensive, and algorithms incapable of navigating messy physical reality, a carbon-based frame of bone, muscle, and nerve fibers was simply the cheapest, most adaptable actuator money could buy.
On an actuary’s ledger, a laborer’s severance liability and workplace compensation payout were far cheaper than a five-year maintenance retainer on an imported robotic arm.
Thus, however degraded one’s existence was, the laborer retained one tragic prerogative: by liquidating bodily integrity and discounting their lifespan, they could pry open a narrow doorway to basic survival. As long as you had the stomach to grind your own tissue to dust, the vast economic apparatus was forced to reserve a blood-stained dividend for you.
You had worth, because your life could still be priced.
The Silicon Ledger: From Exploited to Redundant # The true horror of modern automation is not that it intensifies exploitation, but that capital has abruptly realized it no longer has any interest in exploiting carbon-based flesh at all.
This is a silent, unsparing replacement of fundamental units of account.
A six-axis industrial manipulator coated in Teflon stamps sheet metal unceasingly through the graveyard shift. It will never lose half a palm to a drowsy nod at four in the morning, nor will it drag a factory into six months of contentious labor arbitration over permanent disability. Lidar pods and explosion-proof chassis navigate mine galleries heavy with firedamp and coal dust; they demand neither supplemental oxygen nor heat-stroke stipends, and they will never organize a protest at the factory gates when the fiscal year ends. Even the four-wheeled autonomous delivery cart humming down a rain-swept boulevard glides across slick asphalt with ruthless poise. It never runs yellow lights, never shivers under drenched polyester, and its untimely demise under a dump truck produces no viral outrage on social media.
Viewed purely through engineering efficiency and balance-sheet thermodynamics, the human body is an embarrassing constellation of design flaws: It demands a constant thirty-seven degrees Celsius; it requires perpetual carbohydrate input; it lapses into eight hours of comatose vulnerability each day; it is erratic, emotionally fragile, and structurally brittle. Worst of all, it comes wrapped in legal liabilities and moral encumbrances.
The moment the amortized marginal cost of silicon fell below the subsistence cost of feeding a human body, capital severed its ties with flesh without looking back.
This is not a humanitarian awakening. It is not capital suddenly growing a conscience and sparing laborers from hardship. It is an algorithmic balance-sheet optimization: why negotiate with the unpredictable liabilities of biological life when you can simply write off depreciation on a fixed asset?
In earlier eras, the tragedy was that human beings were treated like machines. The contemporary dead end is that machines have proven themselves far better at being machines than humans ever were.
Laborers have been stripped of the qualification to offer their bodies as collateral. In Immortality Is Just Eternal Loneliness, technology attempts to dissolve the boundaries of mortality at the apex of society; yet at the bottom, technology has already executed the brain-death of manual labor in the market.
The Evaporation of the Buffer # Those ensconced in climate-controlled corner offices, sipping cold brew, often comfort the public with the polished axioms of orthodox economics: “History proves that every technological leap eliminates outdated roles only to birth vast new categories of employment—robot technicians, AI data labelers, workflow supervisors.”
This patronizing homily sounds like telling an aging miner with end-stage silicosis to get certified in prompt engineering.
Over the past decade, the millions displaced from heavy industry and construction retreated into the city’s capillary networks: food delivery, ride-hailing, courier sorting, loading docks. This sprawling gig economy acted as a massive societal sponge, soaking up every worker cast aside by technological disruption.
Now, that sponge is being wrung dry.
At midnight on a rain-drenched intersection, neon signage bleeds across cold, wet asphalt. A delivery courier stands by the corrugated shutter of a convenience store, soaked through, his rancid rain jacket plastered against his back. Cold rainwater trickles down his helmet visor into his collar. He stares at his phone, watching delivery fees slashed in real time by dispatch algorithms that know his exact shivering speed—all while an autonomous pod hums smoothly around the corner. Facing this systemic machine, personal philosophies on navigating technological uncertainty crumble into frail intellectual posturing.
The system is not creating a more dignified future; it is simply executing a final clearance of biological friction.
When Dying in the Pit Becomes an Expired Privilege # Here lies the most grotesque paradox a mild cynic can bear witness to:
Statistically speaking, the modern world has never looked more sanitary or humane. Coal mine fatalities have hit record lows; falls from construction scaffolding have plummeted; acute industrial poisonings are now statistical anomalies. The governmental white papers are pristine, smelling faintly of fresh ink.
Yet if you walk along the overpass of an industrial county town on any given Tuesday afternoon:
You will find men who once welded girders and fastened rivets crouching on grease-streaked curbs. Dressed in faded camouflage work jackets, engine grime permanently etched beneath their fingernails, they silently pass around cheap filterless cigarettes.
Their bodies are intact. Their breathing is steady. Their limbs are whole. They did not drown in an underground flood, did not plunge from thirty stories, and did not leave their fingers beneath a hydraulic press.
They are alive.
It is simply that not a single soul has any use for them.
For the first time in human memory, the working class has lost even the grim consolation of trading their lifespan for a bowl of rice. Once, poor men feared death because their mortality was the only asset they owned; today, they fear survival, because their flesh has been reclassified as surplus material.
That is the true chill of the machine age: No one is whipping you. No one is exploiting you. No one is even cursing you. They have merely bolted the iron doors of the assembly line, hooked the high-voltage cables to the servo banks, and turned away with indifferent grace—
To inform you that not even your life is required anymore.
summary:
The presentation slides at tech keynotes are always immaculate. Bathed in cool hues of cyan and clean white, tailored executives gesture smoothly beneath the spotlights, unveiling high-frame-rate b-roll of six-axis robotic arms dancing across cleanrooms and unmanned shearers cleaving coal seams in the bowels of the earth. The official press releases are draped in immaculate corporate dignity: “Zero-Harm Production,” “Automated Hazard Mitigation,” “Upgrading the Workforce Through Intelligent Infrastructure.”
Applause ripples through the auditorium. Commentators celebrate a triumph of humanitarian progress: human beings will no longer be crushed under collapsing rock faces, nor will they gamble their marrow against the freezing crosswinds of high-rise scaffolding just to secure their next meal.
title: Not Even Your Life Is Wanted: The Lost Bargaining Chip in the Machine Age

content:
Selected cover of the Berkshire shareholder letter To My Fellow Shareholders:
I will no longer be writing Berkshire’s annual report or talking endlessly at the annual meeting. As the British would say, I’m “going quiet.”
Sort of.
Greg Abel will become the boss at yearend. He is a great manager, a tireless worker and an honest communicator. Wish him an extended tenure.
I will continue talking to you and my children about Berkshire via my annual Thanksgiving message. Berkshire’s individual shareholders are a very special group who are unusually generous in sharing their gains with others less fortunate. I enjoy the chance to keep in touch with you. Indulge me this year as I first reminisce a bit. After that, I will discuss the plans for distribution of my Berkshire shares. Finally, I will offer a few business and personal observations.
As Thanksgiving approaches, I’m grateful and surprised by my luck in being alive at 95. When I was young, this outcome did not look like a good bet. Early on, I nearly died.
It was 1938 and Omaha hospitals were then thought of by its citizens as either Catholic or Protestant, a classification that seemed natural at the time.
Our family doctor, Harley Hotz, was a friendly Catholic who made house calls toting a black bag. Dr. Hotz called me Skipper and never charged much for his visits. When I experienced a bad bellyache in 1938, Dr. Hotz came by and, after probing a bit, told me I would be OK in the morning.
He then went home, had dinner and played a little bridge. Dr. Hotz couldn’t, however, get my somewhat peculiar symptoms out of his mind and later that night he dispatched me to St. Catherine’s Hospital for an emergency appendectomy. During the next three weeks, I felt like I was in a nunnery, and began enjoying my new “podium.” I liked to talk – yes, even then – and the nuns embraced me.
To top things off, Miss Madsen, my third-grade teacher, told my 30 classmates to each write me a letter. I probably threw away the letters from the boys but read and reread those from the girls; hospitalization had its rewards.
The highlight of my recovery – which actually was dicey for much of the first week – was a gift from my wonderful Aunt Edie. She brought me a very professional-looking fingerprinting set, and I promptly fingerprinted all of my attending nuns. (I was probably the first Protestant kid they had seen at St. Catherine’s and they didn’t know what to expect.)
My theory – totally nutty, of course – was that someday a nun would go bad and the FBI would find that they had neglected to fingerprint nuns. The FBI and its director, J. Edgar Hoover, had become revered by Americans in the 1930s, and I envisioned Mr. Hoover, himself, coming to Omaha to inspect my invaluable collection. I further fantasized that J. Edgar and I would quickly identify and apprehend the wayward nun. National fame seemed certain.
Obviously, my fantasy never materialized. But, ironically, some years later it became clear that I should have fingerprinted J. Edgar himself as he became disgraced for misusing his post.
Well, that was Omaha in the 1930s, when a sled, a bicycle, a baseball glove and an electric train were coveted by me and my friends. Let’s look at a few other kids from that era, who grew up very nearby and greatly influenced my life but of whom I was for long unaware.
I’ll begin with Charlie Munger, my best pal for 64 years. In the 1930s, Charlie lived a block away from the house I have owned and occupied since 1958.
Early on, I missed befriending Charlie by a whisker. Charlie, 6 ⅔ years older than I, worked in the summer of 1940 at my grandfather’s grocery store, earning $2 for a 10-hour day. (Thrift runs deep in Buffett blood.) The following year I did similar work at the store, but I never met Charlie until 1959 when he was 35 and I was 28.
After serving in World War II, Charlie graduated from Harvard Law and then moved permanently to California. Charlie, however, forever talked of his early years in Omaha as formative. For more than 60 years, Charlie had a huge impact on me and could not have been a better teacher and protective “big brother.” We had differences but never had an argument. “I told you so” was not in his vocabulary.
In 1958, I bought my first and only home. Of course, it was in Omaha, located about two miles from where I grew up (loosely defined), less than two blocks from my in-laws, about six blocks from the Buffett grocery store and a 6-7-minute drive from the office building where I have worked for 64 years.
Let’s move on to another Omahan, Stan Lipsey. Stan sold the Omaha Sun Newspapers (weeklies) to Berkshire in 1968 and a decade later moved to Buffalo at my request. The Buffalo Evening News, owned by a Berkshire affiliate, was then locked in a battle to the death with its morning competitor who published Buffalo’s only Sunday paper. And we were losing.
Stan eventually built our new Sunday product, and for some years our paper – formerly hemorrhaging cash – earned over 100% annually (pre-tax) on our $33 million investment. This was important money to Berkshire in the early 1980s.
Stan grew up about five blocks from my home. One of Stan’s neighbors was Walter Scott, Jr. Walter, you will remember, brought MidAmerican Energy to Berkshire in 1999. He was also a valued Berkshire director until his death in 2021 and a very close friend. Walter was Nebraska’s philanthropic leader for decades and both Omaha and the state carries his imprint.
Walter attended Benson High School, which I was scheduled to attend as well – until my dad surprised everyone in 1942 by beating a four-term incumbent in a Congressional race. Life is full of surprises.
Wait, there’s more.
In 1959, Don Keough and his young family lived in a home located directly across the street from my house and about 100 yards away from where the Munger family had lived. Don was then a coffee salesman but was destined to become president of Coca-Cola as well as a devoted director of Berkshire.
When I met Don, he was earning $12,000 a year while he and his wife Mickie were raising five children, all destined for Catholic schools (with tuition requirements).
Our families became fast friends. Don came from a farm in northwest Iowa and graduated from Omaha’s Creighton University. Early on, he married Mickie, an Omaha girl. After joining Coke, Don went on to become legendary around the globe.
In 1985, when Don was president of Coke, the company launched its ill-fated New Coke. Don made a famous speech in which he apologized to the public and reinstated “Old” Coke. This change of heart took place after Don explained that Coke incoming mail addressed to “Supreme Idiot” was promptly delivered to his desk. His “withdrawal” speech is a classic and can be viewed on YouTube. He cheerfully acknowledged that, in truth, the Coca-Cola product belonged to the public and not to the company. Sales subsequently soared.
You can watch Don on CharlieRose.com in a wonderful interview. (Tom Murphy and Kay Graham have a couple of gems as well.) Like Charlie Munger, Don forever remained a Midwestern boy, enthusiastic, friendly and American to the core.
Finally, Ajit Jain, born and raised in India, as well as Greg Abel, our Canadian CEO-to-be, each lived in Omaha for several years late in the 20th Century. Indeed, in the 1990s, Greg lived only a few blocks away from me on Farnam Street, though we never met at the time.
Can it be that there is some magic ingredient in Omaha’s water?
I lived a few teenage years in Washington, DC (when my dad was in Congress) and in 1954 I took what I thought would be a permanent job in Manhattan. There I was treated wonderfully by Ben Graham and Jerry Newman and made many life-long friends. New York had unique assets – and still does. Nevertheless, in 1956, after only 1½ years, I returned to Omaha, never to wander again.
Subsequently, my three children, as well as several grandchildren, were raised in Omaha. My children always attended public schools (graduating from the same high school that educated my dad (class of 1921), my first wife, Susie (class of 1950) as well as Charlie, Stan Lipsey, Irv and Ron Blumkin, who were key to growing Nebraska Furniture Mart, and Jack Ringwalt (class of 1923), who founded National Indemnity and sold it to Berkshire in 1967 where it became the base upon which our huge P/C operation was constructed.
Our country has many great companies, great schools, great medical facilities and each definitely has its own special advantages along with talented people. But I feel very lucky to have had the good fortune to make many lifelong friends, to meet both of my wives, to receive a great start in education at public schools, to meet many interesting and friendly adult Omahans when I was very young, and to make a wide variety of friends in the Nebraska National Guard. In short, Nebraska has been home.
Looking back I feel that both Berkshire and I did better because of our base in Omaha than if I had resided anywhere else. The center of the United States was a very good place to be born, to raise a family, and to build a business. Through dumb luck, I drew a ridiculously long straw at birth.
Now let’s move on to my advanced age. My genes haven’t been particularly helpful – the family’s all-time record for longevity (admittedly family records get fuzzy as you work backwards) was 92 until I came along. But I have had wise, friendly and dedicated Omaha doctors, starting with Harley Hotz, and continuing to this day. At least three times, my life has been saved, each with doctors based within a few miles from my home. (I have given up fingerprinting nurses, however. You can get away with many eccentricities at 95 . . . . . but there are limits.)
Those who reach old age need a huge dose of good luck, daily escaping banana peels, natural disasters, drunk or distracted drivers, lightning strikes, you name it.
But Lady Luck is fickle and – no other term fits – wildly unfair. In many cases, our leaders and the rich have received far more than their share of luck – which, too often, the recipients prefer not to acknowledge. Dynastic inheritors have achieved lifetime financial independence the moment they emerged from the womb, while others have arrived, facing a hell-hole during their early life or, worse, disabling physical or mental infirmities that rob them of what I have taken for granted. In many heavily-populated parts of the world, I would likely have had a miserable life and my sisters would have had one even worse.
I was born in 1930 healthy, reasonably intelligent, white, male and in America. Wow! Thank you, Lady Luck. My sisters had equal intelligence and better personalities than I but faced a much different outlook. Lady Luck continued to drop by during much of my life, but she has better things to do than work with those in their 90s. Luck has its limits.
Father Time, to the contrary, now finds me more interesting as I age. And he is undefeated; for him, everyone ends up on his score card as “wins.” When balance, sight, hearing and memory are all on a persistently downward slope, you know Father Time is in the neighborhood.
I was late in becoming old – its onset materially varies – but once it appears, it is not to be denied.
To my surprise, I generally feel good. Though I move slowly and read with increasing difficulty, I am at the office five days a week where I work with wonderful people. Occasionally, I get a useful idea or am approached with an offer we might not otherwise have received. Because of Berkshire’s size and because of market levels, ideas are few – but not zero.
My unexpected longevity, however, has unavoidable consequences of major importance to my family and the achievement of my charitable objectives.
Let’s explore them.
What Comes Next
My children are all above normal retirement age, having reached 72, 70 and 67. It would be a mistake to wager that all three – now at their peak in many respects – will enjoy my exceptional luck in delayed aging. To improve the probability that they will dispose of what will essentially be my entire estate before alternate trustees replace them, I need to step up the pace of lifetime gifts to their three foundations. My children are now at their prime in respect to experience and wisdom but have yet to enter old age. That “honeymoon” period will not last forever.
Fortunately, a course correction is easy to execute. There is, however, one additional factor to consider: I would like to keep a significant amount of “A” shares until Berkshire shareholders develop the comfort with Greg that Charlie and I long enjoyed. That level of confidence shouldn’t take long. My children are already 100% behind Greg as are the Berkshire directors.
All three children now have the maturity, brains, energy and instincts to disburse a large fortune. They will also have the advantage of being above ground when I am long gone and, if necessary, can adopt policies both anticipatory and reactive to federal tax policies or other developments affecting philanthropy. They may well need to adapt to a significantly changing world around them. Ruling from the grave does not have a great record, and I have never had an urge to do so.
Fortunately, all three children received a dominant dosage of their genes from their mother. As the decades have passed, I have also become a better model for their thinking and behavior. I will never, however, achieve parity with their mother.
My children have three alternate trustees in case of any premature deaths or disabilities. The alternates are not ranked or tied to a specific child. All three are exceptional humans and wise in the ways of the world. They have no conflicting motives.
I have assured my children that they do not need to perform miracles nor fear failures or disappointments. These are inevitable, and I have made my share. They simply need to improve somewhat upon what generally is achieved by government activities and/or private philanthropy, recognizing these other methods of redistribution of wealth have shortcomings as well.
Early on, I contemplated various grand philanthropic plans. Though I was stubborn, these did not prove feasible. During my many years, I’ve also watched ill-conceived wealth transfers by political hacks, dynastic choices and, yes, inept or quirky philanthropists.
If my children simply do a decent job, they can be certain that their mother and I would be pleased. Their instincts are good and they each have had years of practice with very small sums initially that have been irregularly increased to more than $500 million annually.
All three like working long hours to help others, each in their own way.
The acceleration of my lifetime gifts to my children’s foundations in no way reflects any change in my views about Berkshire’s prospects. Greg Abel has more than met the high expectations I had for him when I first thought he should be Berkshire’s next CEO. He understands many of our businesses and personnel far better than I now do, and he is a very fast learner about matters many CEOs don’t even consider. I can’t think of a CEO, a management consultant, an academic, a member of government – you name it – that I would select over Greg to handle your savings and mine.
Greg understands, for example, far more about both the upside potential and the dangers of our P/C insurance business than do a great many long-time P/C executives. My hope is that his health remains good for several decades. With a little luck, Berkshire should require only five or six CEOs over the next century. It should particularly avoid those whose goal is to retire at 65, to become look-at-me rich or to initiate a dynasty.
One unpleasant reality: Occasionally, a wonderful and loyal CEO of the parent or a subsidiary will succumb to dementia, Alzheimer’s or another debilitating and long-term disease.
Charlie and I encountered this problem several times and failed to act. This failure can be a huge mistake. The Board must be alert to this possibility at the CEO level and the CEO must be alert to the possibility at subsidiaries. This is easier said than done; I could cite a few examples from the past at major companies. Directors should be alert and speak up is all that I can advise.
During my lifetime, reformers sought to embarrass CEOs by requiring the disclosure of the compensation of the boss compared to what was being paid to the average employee. Proxy statements promptly ballooned to 100-plus pages compared to 20 or less earlier.
But the good intentions didn’t work; instead they backfired. Based on the majority of my observations – the CEO of company “A” looked at his competitor at company “B” and subtly conveyed to his board that he should be worth more. Of course, he also boosted the pay of directors and was careful who he placed on the compensation committee. The new rules produced envy, not moderation.
The ratcheting took on a life of its own. What often bothers very wealthy CEOs – they are human, after all – is that other CEOs are getting even richer. Envy and greed walk hand in hand. And what consultant ever recommended a serious cut in CEO compensation or board payments?
In aggregate, Berkshire’s businesses have moderately better-than-average prospects, led by a few non-correlated and sizable gems. However, a decade or two from now, there will be many companies that have done better than Berkshire; our size takes its toll.
Berkshire has less chance of a devastating disaster than any business I know. And, Berkshire has a more shareholder-conscious management and board than almost any company with which I am familiar (and I’ve seen a lot). Finally, Berkshire will always be managed in a manner that will make its existence an asset to the United States and eschew activities that would lead it to become a supplicant. Over time, our managers should grow quite wealthy – they have important responsibilities – but do not have the desire for dynastic or look-at-me wealth.
Our stock price will move capriciously, occasionally falling 50% or so as has happened three times in 60 years under present management. Don’t despair; America will come back and so will Berkshire shares.
A Few Final Thoughts
One perhaps self-serving observation. I’m happy to say I feel better about the second half of my life than the first. My advice: Don’t beat yourself up over past mistakes – learn at least a little from them and move on. It is never too late to improve. Get the right heroes and copy them. You can start with Tom Murphy; he was the best.
Remember Alfred Nobel, later of Nobel Prize fame, who – reportedly – read his own obituary that was mistakenly printed when his brother died and a newspaper got mixed up. He was horrified at what he read and realized he should change his behavior.
Don’t count on a newsroom mix-up: Decide what you would like your obituary to say and live the life to deserve it.
Greatness does not come about through accumulating great amounts of money, great amounts of publicity or great power in government. When you help someone in any of thousands of ways, you help the world. Kindness is costless but also priceless. Whether you are religious or not, it’s hard to beat The Golden Rule as a guide to behavior.
I write this as one who has been thoughtless countless times and made many mistakes but also became very lucky in learning from some wonderful friends how to behave better (still a long way from perfect, however). Keep in mind that the cleaning lady is as much a human being as the Chairman.
I wish all who read this a very happy Thanksgiving. Yes, even the jerks; it’s never too late to change. Remember to thank America for maximizing your opportunities. But it is – inevitably – capricious and sometimes venal in distributing its rewards.
Choose your heroes very carefully and then emulate them. You will never be perfect, but you can always be better.
About Berkshire
Berkshire Hathaway and its subsidiaries engage in diverse business activities including insurance and reinsurance, utilities and energy, freight rail transportation, manufacturing, services and retailing. Common stock of the company is listed on the New York Stock Exchange, trading symbols BRK.A and BRK.B.
Contacts Marc D. Hamburg 402-346-1400

Selected cover of the Berkshire shareholder letter To My Fellow Shareholders:
I will no longer be writing Berkshire’s annual report or talking endlessly at the annual meeting. As the British would say, I’m “going quiet.”
Sort of.
Greg Abel will become the boss at yearend. He is a great manager, a tireless worker and an honest communicator. Wish him an extended tenure.

After reading the recent magazines and reports, my honest advice is this: while these next couple of years are still livable, seize the day and go enjoy yourself.
Two assumptions:
Suppose AI really does keep breaking through and takes over most people’s jobs. Society will inevitably enter a turbulent period of painful adjustment, and nobody knows what will happen.
Suppose AI fails to break through and, in the end, cannot create that much value. Given the enormous leverage the whole world has piled onto AI today, the fallout when the bubble bursts would be no smaller than the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis. Nobody knows what will happen.
So make the most of these two years, while nothing has happened yet.
In the face of such enormous uncertainty about the future, what any individual can contribute is vanishingly small.

The Economist cover, November 8, 2025: Rebalancing the World The Economist has always excelled at using polished prose to gloss over savage fractures, dressing up the disintegration of the postwar free-trade architecture and superpower zero-sum warfare as a dignified “Rebalancing the World.” Peel back the magazine’s glossy rhetoric, however, and one confronts an unyielding reality: the high priests of globalization are boarding up their doors, tariff iron curtains are slamming down, and major economies are locking each other in a death grip over industrial subsidies and zero-sum geopolitical spheres.
Washington’s Enclosure: A Liberal Dirge and Tariff Walls # Washington’s political elite has personally buried what remained of the Bretton Woods consensus it spent half a century erecting. The dogmas once preached as gospel—small government, low tariffs, frictionless factor mobility—have been smashed to dust under the CHIPS Act, the Inflation Reduction Act, and dense reams of unilateral sanctions.
Tariffs are no longer transient bargaining chips; they have become permanent geopolitical trenches. Cross-border supply chains are severed by administrative decree. As detailed in our breakdown of the economic blowback of chip restrictions, the attempt to forcefully onshore advanced foundries and semiconductor ecosystems has purchased little beyond stubborn domestic inflation and massive balance-sheet impairments for American tech giants.
At the core of this anxiety lies the hemorrhaging capacity of federal governance. A thirty-six-trillion-dollar sovereign debt hangs overhead like the sword of Damocles, with net interest payments alone devouring a trillion dollars of public revenue each year. Partisan factions stage perpetual theater on the Capitol steps, turning foreign rivals into all-purpose scapegoats to mask domestic administrative rot. The beacon on the hill has flickered out; in its place stands a harried gatekeeper feverishly boarding up windows against the storm.
Subsidy Cannibalism and the Second Breakout # Across the Pacific, the retirement of land-driven fiscal expansion and the real-estate pillar is complete. In their place stands a total commitment by state capital and command mechanisms toward advanced manufacturing, the new energy triad, and complete supply-chain self-sufficiency.
The political will behind “new quality productive forces” is austere: it prepares for full-scale encirclement and extreme stress. China has pushed industrial output to the red line. Solar arrays, battery storage, and electric vehicles steamroll global markets with insurmountable cost efficiencies, instantly triggering Western tariff walls erected under the banner of “anti-dumping” and “overcapacity.” As explored in our analysis of the rare earth war and geopolitical depth, in zero-sum rivalry, every industrial advantage is immediately politicized into an existential security threat.
Surplus industrial capacity must find an outlet abroad. With North American and European borders slammed shut, Chinese exports course through the arteries of Southeast Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East. This is no gentle corporate globalization; it is a precarious, anxiety-driven breakout under relentless external compression.
Brussels’ Medical Chart: The Old Continent in the Vise # Europe cuts a pathetic figure on this chessboard. The Franco-German engine has splintered over soaring energy bills, defense spending targets, and fiscal austerity limits.
Deprived of cheap Russian pipeline gas and marginalized in both frontier AI foundation models and leading-edge semiconductor lithography, Brussels has degenerated into an obese bureaucratic clearinghouse lacking the barest capacity for geopolitical self-defense. Facing Washington’s tariff extortion on one flank and the crush of Chinese factory efficiency on the other, the European Union’s sole defensive arsenal consists of Byzantine compliance checklists, privacy regulations, and carbon border adjustment taxes.
The fig leaf of European idealism has been shredded. Every metric on the bureaucrat’s medical chart flashes red: trying to fund an unsustainable welfare net while coerced by NATO mandates into diverting two percent or more of GDP into arms procurement. Squeezed between two continental titans, the Old Continent finds itself paralyzed and stripped of pride.
Compute Arms Races and the Liquidity Reckoning # The tech sector’s delirium is wearing off. Generative AI was sold across Wall Street and Silicon Valley as the ultimate antidote to structural productivity decay. Yet computing clusters funded by hundreds of billions in capital expenditure devour staggering quantities of power and water while failing to generate self-sustaining cash flows.
Tech monopolies hoard enterprise silicon to build anticompetitive moats, while downstream startups collapse under crushing inference fees and arid unit economics. The so-called technological revolution has devolved into a standard-issue fixed-asset arms race among monopolists playing a winner-take-all game.
Simultaneously, the decade of cheap liquidity is definitively over. Central bank rate paths hesitate between sticky inflation and looming stagnation, forcing global markets to reprice every risk asset from scratch. Heavily indebted sovereigns and cash-burning balance sheets face brutal, unsentimental liquidation.
At this global table, the old rules are dead and no new covenant exists. Every player has swapped their cards for bare steel, coldly calculating which rival at the table will bleed out first.

The President’s Contradictory Posture # In public, President Trump has spent weeks deriding Zohran Mamdani as an extremist, a communist, and a threat to New York City. He has also insisted that he is “much better looking” than the 34-year-old Mamdani.
But in private, according to two people who disclosed the president’s remarks on condition of anonymity, Trump has described the New York City mayor-elect as a talented politician — sharp-minded and quick with an argument.
For all that grudging admiration, the two men appear headed for a showdown — the young democratic socialist squaring off against a president who long ago sized him up as the perfect target. To Trump, the mayor-elect embodies the Democratic opposition; hours after Mamdani pulled off his seemingly impossible victory, the president called Democrats “crazy” — and “Mamdani, or whatever the hell his name is” just as bad.
The Federal-City Money Game # Trump’s aides and allies acknowledge that Mamdani and New York City are likely to become the president’s next round of targets, though some caution that because Trump owns multiple real estate assets in New York, the city’s economic prosperity is bound up with his own vested interests. On Wednesday, Trump even said he might “help him out a little,” because he wants New York City to succeed.
Even so, the president has threatened to withhold federal funds, giving the city nothing “beyond the minimum required by law.” In fact, apart from a few narrow exceptions, he has no authority to withhold funding Congress has already approved. (The administration previously tried to withhold federal funds from some cities over immigration policy, and repeatedly lost in court.)
The federal government provides New York City with dozens of grants, covering health care, transportation, law enforcement and more. If the administration withholds any one of those expected allocations, litigation is close to certain.
The New Mayor Hits Back Hard # Mamdani, for his part, looks ready for the fight. In his victory speech he challenged Trump head-on, vowing to strike back against federal interference in New York’s internal affairs.
“Donald Trump, I know you’re watching, and I have a message for you,” he taunted the TV-loving president. “Turn it up.”
(White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt later confirmed that Trump had indeed been watching the speech.)
Mamdani says he will not be cowed by the president’s threats, and that New York City will provide the playbook for defeating Trump and his political movement.
“Listen to me, President Trump,” he said. “If you come after one of us, you will have to go through all of us.”
To fight the Trump administration, Mamdani has little recourse beyond lawsuits. The mayor-elect has pledged to hire 200 more lawyers for the city’s legal department — partly, precisely, to fend off what his campaign called “presidential abuse of power.”
The “Perfect Opponent” on the Political Chessboard # In his second term, Trump has repeatedly shown a willingness to use the powers of the federal government to settle scores with political enemies, at times even with eagerness. He has stripped away billions in federal grants, aiming squarely at Democratic-governed states and cities like New York City; he has sent the National Guard into Democratic cities against their will; and he has directed the Justice Department to prosecute political opponents, including New York’s attorney general.
But some of the president’s allies say privately that Mamdani’s victory may actually be good for Trump, letting him reuse the long-standing routine he has deployed to demonize Democratic leaders — as with former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, and the Democratic billionaire backer George Soros — and thereby advance his political agenda.
Ever since Mamdani’s upset win in the Democratic primary, Trump and his allies have cast him as the face of the party’s future, working to paint the Democrats as an extremist force. On Wednesday, when Trump attacked Democrats for allowing transgender women and girls to compete in women’s sports, he lumped Mamdani into the same camp.
“He thinks it’s great to have men playing in women’s sports,” Trump said.
Facing Trump’s policies targeting transgender people, Mamdani has pledged to defend the rights of transgender New Yorkers and make New York a “sanctuary city” for LGBTQ residents. He has yet to take an explicit position on the athlete question; his spokesperson pointed only to his past remarks.
The Balancing Act Between Cooperation and Confrontation # Mamdani calls himself a democratic socialist, not a communist. He seems unafraid of going toe-to-toe with the president, and on Wednesday morning he played down the criticism that his victory speech had deliberately provoked Trump.
“If the president is willing to work together and deliver on his campaign promises of lowering the price of groceries or the cost of living, I will work with him,” the mayor-elect said in an NY1 interview. “But if he wants to come after the people of this city, then I will stand up and defend them every step of the way.”
David Axelrod, the Democratic strategist and longtime adviser to President Obama, said some of Mamdani’s remarks about Trump amounted to “unnecessary schoolyard taunting.”
“I don’t think there’s much point in getting into online taunting matches with Trump, but when he has essentially declared war on this city, pushing back hard is necessary,” he said. “The key question is: how do you challenge the president while still holding on to the idea of a mayor who serves the entire city?”
Trump is a New Yorker born and bred, and he has always paid close attention to the city’s affairs. His advisers tried to intervene in the election to block Mamdani and failed; last year Trump campaigned for president in New York City repeatedly, even though the city’s voters reliably back Democrats.
Which is why some of Trump’s allies in New York are encouraging him to take a more polished approach to the city.
John Catsimatidis, the New York grocery and oil billionaire, said he has told the president not to withhold money that would help the people of New York, and that he sees no need for the president to send the military into the city; instead, he has suggested Trump have the federal government closely monitor all federal money allocated to New York City.
“They’re not going to give him money and let him spend it any way he wants,” he added. “I think the president will be watching closely, because he cares about New York.”
summary:
The President’s Contradictory Posture # In public, President Trump has spent weeks deriding Zohran Mamdani as an extremist, a communist, and a threat to New York City. He has also insisted that he is “much better looking” than the 34-year-old Mamdani.
But in private, according to two people who disclosed the president’s remarks on condition of anonymity, Trump has described the New York City mayor-elect as a talented politician — sharp-minded and quick with an argument.
title: Trump vs the New NYC Mayor: Prelude to a Political Storm

The Rare-Earth War The Rare-Earth War # —— China’s strategic confidence and resource sovereignty amid the reshaping of global geopolitics
Preface # I studied geology at China University of Geosciences. As an undergraduate, as part of an academic activity organized by the university, I wrote a short paper titled “The Rare-Earth War.” Back then, the “war” was mostly a metaphor in the academic sense, an exploration of the relationship between resource competition and technological rivalry. Many years on, the world has shifted beyond recognition, and the scenarios once argued on paper are now playing out in reality. Taking up the pen again to rewrite “The Rare-Earth War” fills me with emotion.
China: The Global Manufacturing Power Holding the Rare Earths Initiative # Against a backdrop of international turbulence, China — on the strength of long-term industrial accumulation and technical capability — holds a firm dominant position in the rare earth metals and magnets market. These rare earth materials are the core inputs of missiles, fighter jets, drones, submarines and even the new-energy industries, earning them the name “vitamins of industry.”
Decades of development have given China’s rare earths industry a complete chain running from mining and smelting to fine processing. It is precisely this systemic advantage that gives China an irreplaceable position in the global high-tech supply chain. The advantage was not won overnight; it is the fruit of long-term planning and technological self-reliance.
Europe’s Anxiety and Dependence # Facing increasingly severe geopolitical challenges, the countries of Europe are scrambling to rearm and reduce their dependence on outside powers. Yet the reality is plain to see: about 98% of the EU’s critical rare earths imports depend on China — a degree of dependence even higher than America’s 80%.
Although Brussels loudly proclaims “strategic autonomy” and has rolled out its so-called Critical Raw Materials Act, hoping to build a domestic mining and refining system, analysts broadly agree that the process will take at least 8 to 12 years. Europe’s rearmament plans, meanwhile, demand completed capability gains before 2030 — and that gap in time turns “autonomy” into an idealistic slogan.
The EU hopes to obtain a “general export license” in cooperation with the Chinese side to ease supply pressure, but whether that can land, and how long it can hold, remain uncertain. Europe has fallen into strategic anxiety — pursuing security while being leashed by resource realities.
China’s Lawful Defensive Measures # In April this year, the United States moved first with hefty tariffs, and China took lawful countermeasures, placing exports of certain rare earths and magnets under licensing management. This policy is not retaliation but the necessary choice of national security and resource strategy.
Rare earths are strategic resources, used widely across high-tech and military fields. The Chinese government has a responsibility to ensure that the export of these resources accords with international law and the national interest, and to prevent their use in projects that would harm China’s security. This is not only protection for the country itself but also a necessary step to keep the global supply chain stable.
At the same time, China has always remained open, willing to hold dialogue with partners including the EU. The Chinese side stresses that cooperation should be built on equality and mutual trust, not on political pressure or unilateral demands.
The West’s “Rare Earths Anxiety” and Its Reality Trap # For all that America and Europe proclaim “de-risking,” no country in the world can build a rare earths supply chain to rival China’s in the short term. The US invests heavily in rare earths companies, yet its ore still has to be shipped to China for refining. Europe, even with enormous sums committed, runs headlong into the realities of technology barriers and high costs.
The contest over rare earths looks on the surface like a supply problem; in substance it is a competition over industry, technology and strategic autonomy. By commanding the key mineral resources, China has secured its national safety and technological independence, and has acted as a stabilizer of the global supply chain. Conversely, the West’s institutional prejudice against China and its containment designs will only deepen its own industrial anxiety.
Conclusion: Resource Sovereignty and Shared Gains # As a European scholar has put it: “Defense autonomy begins with materials autonomy.” But true autonomy is not closed-off self-protection; it is built on long-term accumulation, rational development and open cooperation.
China is not the starter of the rare-earths war, but a defender of resource sovereignty and an advocate of global cooperation. In an era of constantly reshaping international relations, China’s rare earths policy reflects the strategic composure of a responsible major power — safeguarding its own core interests while advancing the security and sustainable development of global supply chains.
The rare-earths war is, in the final analysis, a contest of technology and strategic will. And in this contest over the shape of the future order, China already stands on the high ground of initiative, confidence and reason.
